clusters.name: Maintenance Failure Procedure

clusters.name: Repository Failure Recovery
clusters.description: How planned, unplanned, and stale-state failures are tolerated, repaired, or introduced operationally.

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Failure Recovery limit the options available on Repository Replica Count and Sizing
relations.rationale: The reboot procedure limits simultaneous copy loss to preserve availability and quorum during maintenance.

values.label: Quiesced rolling rack reboots
values.description: Servers finish outstanding reads, then reboot sequentially by rack to reduce service interruption.

values.label: Rack-level availability zones
values.description: Racks define failure and maintenance boundaries for rolling operations.

values.label: Bounded parallel reboots
values.description: No more than five quiesced servers reboot simultaneously within a rack.

values.label: Chaos-monkey file-server testing
values.description: Random single-node failure testing is avoided because it would interrupt long-running reads.

values.label: Unplanned server unplugging
values.description: Abrupt server removal is rejected because it interrupts reads and can eliminate remaining failure tolerance.

values.label: Automated repository repair
values.description: Unhealthy repository copies trigger repair jobs intended to restore them rapidly.

values.label: Stale-routing fallback
values.description: Routing state may become stale after failures without invalidating service; the repository can be materialized on the selected host.

values.label: Combined heartbeat and real-traffic monitoring
values.description: Repository health is assessed using both periodic heartbeats and failures observed during real application requests.

values.label: Heartbeat-only monitoring
values.description: Only periodic heartbeat checks are used to decide whether a repository server is healthy.

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: A server is removed from routing only after three consecutive request failures.

values.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
values.description: Reverting writes that fail to achieve identical application at a replica majority.

values.label: Exclusion of losing replicas
values.description: Removing replicas on the losing side of a write vote from reads and writes until repair.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: Rebuilding failed replicas anywhere in the cluster from any surviving replica.

values.label: Periodic replica-count reconciliation
values.description: Periodically restoring each repository to its desired replica count after failures or shortages.

values.label: Retirement through active-replica exclusion
values.description: Removing a retiring server from active replica counts while retaining it as a fallback and replacing it through repair.

values.label: Application-server-local failure views
values.description: Each application server maintains its own view of unavailable file servers.

values.label: Development interruption cost from repository unavailability
values.description: Repository access and CI failures impose substantial productivity losses, motivating reliability-oriented failure recovery.

values.label: Delayed failure recognition
values.description: Failures remain usable long enough to cause redirected operations before detection completes.

values.label: Variable quiescing duration
values.description: Maintenance may wait seconds to hours while active reads drain.

values.description: Users selectively populate additional directories as their development tasks require them.

These axes matter directly to scaling very large repositories and very many clients, and cannot be added as values of the existing server authority, placement, routing, replication, or packfile-compaction axes without conflating different architectural decisions. Partial clone for reduced clone and fetch cost
GVFS Protocol in the standard Git client
Git protocol for repositories without GVFS infrastructure
Real application traffic as health checking
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers sparse working trees, background maintenance, Git object layout, repository authority, replication, routing, and failure repair, so most open codes are already subsumed. However, several relevant architectural axes are missing. First, there is no client feature-integration and activation dimension covering custom Git distributions versus upstream/core Git, automatic performance configuration, and compatibility-oriented defaults. Second, reduced initial materialization is represented only as an outcome; the distinct client/server object-acquisition protocol choice—partial clone versus GVFS Protocol versus ordinary Git protocol, including the need for a co-located GVFS cache—is not captured. Third, Repository Failure Recovery and Access Routing mention healthy nodes and routing around failures, but do not capture the health-observation strategy and its trade-offs: heartbeat-only checks versus real application traffic, failure thresholds, and false-positive removal. Finally, the S3-backed authority model captures the WAL as the authoritative store, but not the independent write-ingestion decision between batching object-storage writes and issuing one S3 write per push. These concepts matter directly to scaling client operation, failure detection, protocol cost, and push throughput, and cannot be added as values of an existing axis without conflating distinct decisions.

uncovered_concepts: Co-located repository copies on local disk
Networked filesystem semantics for Git operations
Networked filesystem performance and correctness failures
saturation_history.rationale: Most codes are covered: checksum computation and verification fit Repository Consistency Semantics; sparse working-tree behavior fits Client Working-Tree Scaling; pack maintenance fits Git Object Indexing and Maintenance; quorum, repair, placement, and coordination codes fit the existing replication, failure-recovery, mutation-coordination, and authority dimensions. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct decision about replica catch-up and propagation signaling, so Gossip UDP replication signaling is not fully captured by the existing commit or routing dimensions. It also lacks a server-side application and repository-storage-substrate dimension. The Rails monolith code concerns application decomposition and horizontal scaling, while the local-disk, filesystem-distribution, and NFS codes concern whether Git repositories use co-located local storage or a networked filesystem. These are distinct from repository authority, placement, routing, and object layout: they determine the filesystem semantics, performance, correctness, and development-cost trade-offs of hosting Git at scale.

Most open codes are covered. Client compression, filesystem monitoring, sparse checkout, partial clone, source/build-directory layout, background maintenance, and Scalar-to-core-Git integration are represented by dimensions 9, 12, 13, and 14. Failure-detection and failover details are absorbable by Repository Failure Recovery and Repository Access Routing, while replication count, geography, quorum, latency targets, and read/write trade-offs are covered by Replication Topology, Mutation Coordination, and Consistency Semantics. The clear gaps are (1) a client remote-synchronization policy—specifically scheduled background fetches—and (2) the mechanism and abstraction level used to replicate repository data. The latter is distinct from replica topology and mutation coordination: DRBD block replication versus an application-level Git/rsync-based replication system represents a separate architectural axis.

uncovered_concepts: S3 Express One Zone storage tier
saturation_history.rationale: The minibatch is largely covered. Quiesced maintenance, read draining, withdrawal tolerance, quorum behavior, consistent replication, application-level replication, packfile layout, background/incremental Git maintenance, and consistency-versus-availability trade-offs are represented by the existing failure-recovery, replica-placement, mutation-protocol, repository-consistency, object-storage, and maintenance dimensions. However, the taxonomy does not yet capture the distinct choice of object-storage performance tier for the authoritative WAL (S3 Standard versus S3 Express One Zone). It also lacks an axis for WAL lifecycle compaction and for the placement and distribution of expensive Git repacking: primary-only compaction with compacted-pack distribution versus independent replica-side repacking. These choices materially affect ingestion throughput, recovery cost, CPU consumption, network bandwidth, and availability at scale, and cannot be represented without conflating them with the existing general maintenance or replication axes.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Replication Mechanism
selected_clusters.description: Which mechanism creates and serves consistent repository copies across hosts?

values.label: Application-level repository replication
values.description: Git-aware replication creates and maintains multiple repository copies, with application-level repair and rebalancing rather than relying solely on block-level filesystem mirroring.

includes.label: Application-level Git replication
includes.description: Git and rsync replicate repositories while supporting repair and rebalancing.

values.label: Layered distributed repository replication
values.description: A distributed replication architecture combines repository copies, filesystem or host placement constraints, application-level copying, and scalable consistent serving. It represents the broader multi-layer approach adopted across the more evolved designs.

includes.label: Co-located fileserver replicas
includes.description: Repository copies are kept adjacent to satisfy latency-sensitive replication.

includes.label: DRBD filesystem replication
includes.description: Filesystem block replication is used as the repository-copying mechanism.

includes.label: Application-level Git replication
includes.description: Git and rsync replicate repositories while supporting repair and rebalancing.

includes.label: Horizontally scalable consistent replicas

selected_clusters.name: Repository Replica Count and Sizing
selected_clusters.description: How many replicas are assigned to each repository, and how does replica capacity scale with demand?

values.label: Three-replica configuration
values.description: Each repository has three replicas, providing redundancy while imposing a fixed resource and coordination cost.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica sizing
values.description: Assigning replica counts according to repository load, from one for tiny repositories to hundreds for large monorepositories.

values.label: Reference-update throughput target
values.description: Replication is sized to sustain several reference updates per second per repository.

values.label: Replica-count scalability ceiling
values.description: Increasing replica count worsens push throughput because coordination follows cluster-tail latency.

values.label: Idle replica resource overhead
values.description: Mandatory replicas consume resources even for lightly used repositories.

values.label: Durable highly available repository access
values.description: Multiple copies preserve access and data through server or network failures.

selected_clusters.name: Read Validation and Catch-up
selected_clusters.description: How do replicas validate freshness and catch up before serving repository reads?

values.label: Fully consistent repository views
values.description: Repository views are maintained as mutually consistent representations rather than eventually consistent copies.

values.label: Gossip replication signaling
values.description: Using optimistic UDP gossip to notify replicas of catch-up metadata while relying on authoritative storage for recovery.

values.label: ETag-validated replica reads
values.description: Conditionally verifying a replica against the authoritative WAL index before serving fetches or clones.

values.label: Read-time replica catch-up
values.description: Catching a replica up from a newer authoritative WAL index before serving a read.

values.label: Full checksum recomputation cost
values.description: The cost incurred when logical repository checksums are recomputed from scratch for large reference sets.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
values.description: Maintaining fully consistent replicas imposes substantial implementation complexity.

values.label: Inconsistent-read client and CI failures
values.description: Stale replicas can make post-push clients and CI unable to find commits.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Serving Mechanism

values.description: Separate branch-update authority from distributed endpoints that deliver missing pack objects near clients.

values.label: Co-located GVFS cache-server proxying
values.description: A nearby cache server proxies GVFS requests for large repositories and reduces load on the origin service.

values.label: Git-protocol repository access

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS is deployed without the cache-server resources needed for large-scale operation.

values.label: Three-phase commit

values.label: Consensus-free primary acceptance
values.description: Any server can safely accept a push without elections or fixed primary ownership.

values.label: S3 atomic compare-and-swap

values.label: Advanced consensus coordination

values.label: Majority-based per-write voting
values.description: Having replicas vote directly on write order and accepting a write only after identical application at a majority.

values.label: Single-primary write ordering
values.description: Using one elected primary replica to establish official write order for all replicas.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Write Quorum
selected_clusters.description: How many synchronized replicas must accept a repository write before it is acknowledged or admitted?

values.label: Three-copy push quorum

values.label: Majority write acknowledgment
values.description: Push acceptance waits for acknowledgment from a replica majority.

values.label: Write refusal below replication quorum
values.description: Writes are rejected when required replica commitment cannot be achieved.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions: repository count and sizing (29), read freshness and catch-up (28), host selection (17), serving mechanism (18), and client configuration (13) are separable decisions. The main overlap is between mutation protocol (21) and write quorum (20): 21.5, "Majority-based per-write voting," and 20.4, "Majority write acknowledgment," both present majority acceptance as an alternative, so retain the voting procedure under 21 and keep only the replica-threshold choice under 20. A weaker boundary exists between replication mechanism (31) and read validation/catch-up (28), but their questions—creating copies versus validating and updating them before reads—remain sufficiently different and should not be merged.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many labels and descriptions are concrete, such as 28.3 ETag-validated replica reads and 20.2 minimum-two-replica synchronous quorum, but several dimensions do not ask one clear question covering their values. Dimension 13 Client Performance Configuration mixes activation defaults, Git distribution, core integration, fetch scheduling, status calculation, and commit-graph writes; split or reorganize these existing values into decision-specific dimensions. Dimension 17 Repository Host Selection conflates the location database, hashing algorithm, replica preference, checksum metadata, and serving locality; separate these decision types. Dimension 21 Repository Mutation Protocol similarly mixes commit protocols, primary selection, storage CAS, consensus, and voting. Within dimension 31, 31.1 Application-level repository replication and 31.2 Layered distributed repository replication substantially overlap and should be merged or rewritten to express distinct alternatives. Within dimension 20, 20.2 Minimum-two-replica synchronous quorum and 20.4 Majority write acknowledgment can describe the same policy, so clarify their scopes or consolidate them.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most major areas with multiple candidate decisions: replication and sizing (31, 29), consistency and catch-up (28), serving and caching (18), client scaling (13), host routing (17), mutation coordination (21), and write durability (20). The main coverage gap is that client-side large-repository access and maintenance are bundled into the broad Client Performance Configuration dimension (13); split it into separate questions using the existing values, with 13.1–13.4 for feature delivery/configuration and 13.5–13.7 for background synchronization and maintenance, so both client concerns are explicit decision points. Recovery, repair, and rebalancing are also only embedded in descriptions such as 31.1 and 17.3 rather than represented as a distinct decision point; reorganize those existing values under a recovery/repair question while retaining at least two alternatives. Overall, the existing dimensions provide substantial multi-option coverage, but these areas are less directly represented.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: All nine dimensions are within scope of architectural decisions for Git at scale across servers and clients. Repository replication, replica sizing, read validation, serving mechanisms, host selection, mutation coordination, and write quorums directly address many repositories, large repositories, many users, and failure or throughput concerns; Client Performance Configuration covers the client-side scaling concerns. The outcome values, such as read scaling, durability, and consistency costs, are explicitly permitted by the evaluation steps. No dimension is out of scope or merely tangentially related.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: The taxonomy largely avoids explicit catch-all buckets such as “Other” or “Miscellaneous.” The main issue is value 31.2, “Layered distributed repository replication,” whose description explicitly presents a broad multi-layer approach combining repository copies, placement constraints, application-level copying, and serving rather than one concrete alternative. Drop 31.2 or move its specific mechanisms into the existing replication, read-validation, and host-selection dimensions; the remaining values are specific decisions or outcomes rather than catch-alls.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions mix distinct decision points rather than presenting one question with alternatives. Dimension 28, "Read Validation and Catch-up," should be split into freshness validation/signaling (for example 28.1 versus 28.3) and catch-up initiation (28.2 versus 28.4). Dimension 13, "Client Performance Configuration," combines feature delivery (13.3/13.4), defaults (13.1/13.2), and independent maintenance behaviors (13.5–13.7); split these into separate decisions for the client-side scaling choices. Dimension 17, "Repository Host Selection," combines location metadata (17.1/17.3) with routing and serving-replica selection (17.2/17.4/17.5), so separate those decisions. Dimension 21, "Repository Mutation Protocol," combines replica commit, write ordering, and the S3 synchronization primitive; split it into distinct commit and ordering/coordination decisions. These reorganizations are important for the requested server- and client-side architecture taxonomy for very many, very large repositories and users.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Several dimensions contain multiple decision questions despite the otherwise relevant server/client scaling scope. (1) Dimension 13, Client Performance Configuration, mixes configuration policy (13.1-13.2), implementation/distribution (13.3-13.4), and separate maintenance settings (13.5-13.7); split the first two into decision points with two values each and remove or move the remaining singleton decisions to matching existing dimensions. (2) Dimension 17, Repository Host Selection, combines location mechanisms (17.1-17.2), replica-routing policies (17.4-17.5), and checksum validation metadata (17.3); split the first two groups and move 17.3 to the existing replica-validation decision. (3) Dimension 28, Read Validation and Catch-up, combines consistency/read validation (28.1, 28.3) with catch-up signaling and execution (28.2, 28.4); split those into two dimensions, retaining at least two candidates in each. (4) Dimension 20, Replica Write Quorum, mixes quorum size (20.1, 20.2, 20.4) with admission behavior when quorum is unavailable (20.3, 20.5); split these questions. (5) Dimension 29, Repository Replica Count and Sizing, includes the throughput target 29.3, which is a constraint/target rather than a replica-count alternative; remove it from the candidate decisions. The other dimensions generally have at least two candidate decisions answering a recognizable mechanism or policy question, and outcome values are appropriately distinguishable from candidates.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and the outcome values in dimensions 29, 28, 31, and 17 are described as effects rather than alternatives. However, several mixed values are described as adopted: 31.2 "Layered distributed repository replication" says the approach was adopted, 28.1 "Fully consistent repository views" says views are maintained, 18.4 "Git-protocol repository access" says repositories use it, and 13.3 "Custom Git distribution" says it supplies capabilities. For each, either change the status to accepted if adoption is intended, or rewrite the description to explicitly preserve the source disagreement. No clear duplicate candidate or outcome-as-alternative violation is otherwise evident.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy places nearly all decision-bearing passages under existing dimensions, including client performance configuration (13), replication and sizing (31, 29), serving and host selection (18, 17), and mutation/quorum protocols (21, 20). The main uncovered decision is s03_p07: planned maintenance uses server quiescing so long-running reads finish while writes continue during reboot. Add a planned-maintenance or graceful-shutdown dimension/value for quiescing and write/read handling, supported by s03_p07 (and the rolling-reboot policy in s03_p08).

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many major adopted Spokes choices, including application-level replication (31.1), three replicas and throughput goals (29.1 and 29.3), rendezvous hashing and nearest synchronized reads (17.2 and 17.5), three-phase commit and quorum-based writes (21.1, 20.2, and 20.4), and Scalar's automatic configuration and background fetches (13.1 and 13.5). Missing options requiring revision are: (1) add "Git partial clone" to dimension 18, Repository Serving Mechanism, supported by s04_p01 and s04_p02; (2) add client-maintenance values such as sparse-checkout cone mode, background incremental maintenance/GC, loose-object cleanup, and multi-pack-index maintenance to dimension 13, Client Performance Configuration, supported by s04_p02, s05_p04, s05_p09, and s05_p12; (3) add rejected "block-level filesystem replication" and the rejected distributed-filesystem/packfile approaches to dimension 31, Repository Replication Mechanism, supported by s02_p02, s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05; (4) add a value for coalescing bookkeeping updates and prioritizing user-initiated updates to dimension 21, Repository Mutation Protocol, supported by s02_p06; and (5) add a maintenance-lifecycle dimension covering quiescing before reboot, rolling reboot, and graceful replica retirement, supported by s03_p07, s03_p08, and s03_p09. Dimension 20 also lacks the non-voting geo-replica option described in s02_p06.

criteria.name: Value exclusivity
criteria.description: Each system (source) adopts one value per dimension: the values of a dimension are alternatives, not features used together. Deterministic: computed from the evidence, without a judge.
criteria.reason:
- Dimension 17 'Repository Host Selection': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 17.3 'Continuous checksum routing metadata' and 17.5 'Closest synchronized replica serving' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p07, s01_p09, s02_p05).
- Dimension 20 'Replica Write Quorum': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 20.1 'Three-copy push quorum' and 20.3 'Durability-prioritized write admission' are adopted together by s02, s03 (passages s02_p01, s03_p01, s03_p02).
- Dimension 21 'Repository Mutation Protocol': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 21.1 'Three-phase commit' and 21.4 'Advanced consensus coordination' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p07, s01_p08, s02_p03).
- Dimension 13 'Client Performance Configuration': 2 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 13.1 'Automatic performance configuration' and 13.3 'Custom Git distribution' are adopted together by s04, s05 (passages s04_p01, s04_p02, s05_p01).
Values one source uses together are not alternatives. Split such a dimension into the questions its values answer (every part keeps at least two candidate decisions), move a value to the existing dimension whose question it answers, or merge two values that are the same option.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions relevant to scaling Git repositories, including authority (1), placement (2), object maintenance (6), and failure procedures (7). However, dimension 5, "Replication Topology," overlaps with dimension 4 because value 5.2, "Three-copy push quorum," is an update-coordination choice; move it to dimension 4. Dimension 5 also overlaps with dimension 3, "Repository Request Routing," because value 5.4, "Closest synchronized replica serving," answers how requests select hosts; move it to dimension 3. The remaining replication values can stay in dimension 5 because they concern copy count, roles, and geographic distribution rather than routing or coordination.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions clearly state a design question and most values have distinct, technically specific descriptions; for example, dimension 6 distinguishes single-pack repacking from multi-pack indexes, and dimension 5 clearly separates replica topology from geographic read serving. However, dimension 1, "Repository Authority Model," includes value 1.4, "Fully consistent repository views," which describes a consistency/replication property rather than how authority is established; move it to dimension 4 or revise the dimension to cover consistency semantics. Dimension 3, "Repository Request Routing," includes value 3.4, "Continuous checksum routing metadata," whose description concerns copy-integrity detection rather than host selection; move it to dimension 7 and broaden that dimension's name and description to cover failure detection and repair. Dimension 7, "Maintenance Failure Procedure," does not clearly cover value 7.6, "Automated repository repair," which is remediation rather than failure introduction; rename the dimension to "Server Failure and Maintenance Handling" and update its description. The remaining labels and descriptions are generally distinguishable, though several dimensions combine mechanisms and effects.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents most server-side scaling areas with multiple candidates, including repository authority (1), placement and routing (2–3), update coordination (4), replication (5), large-repository object maintenance (6), and failure handling (7). However, the use case explicitly includes clients, while all decision points are primarily server/storage oriented; dimension 6, "Git Object Maintenance Strategy," does not provide a client-side decision point with alternative client strategies. Also, several dimensions mix alternatives with effects, such as 4.6, 5.5–5.7, and 6.6, so move those outcome values under the decisions they result from to make the candidate sets represent choices more directly.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Dimensions 1–6 are within scope: repository authority, placement, routing, update coordination, replication, and Git object maintenance are architectural decisions directly relevant to scaling repositories and users on hosting servers. Dimension 7, "Maintenance Failure Procedure," is mostly operational procedure and failure testing—such as quiesced rack reboots, bounded reboot counts, and chaos-monkey testing—rather than a repository architecture decision. Drop dimension 7, or move only its architecture-relevant content into dimension 5, "Replication Topology."

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No catch-all dimensions or values are present. The dimensions use specific decision topics, such as Repository Request Routing, Update Coordination Protocol, Git Object Maintenance Strategy, and Maintenance Failure Procedure, and their values identify concrete alternatives or outcomes rather than buckets like “Other” or “Miscellaneous.” No revision is needed for this criterion.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several values are not answers to their named dimensions. Move 1.4 "Fully consistent repository views" from Repository Authority Model to Update Coordination Protocol, since it describes consistency semantics rather than how authority is established. Move 3.4 "Continuous checksum routing metadata" to Maintenance Failure Procedure, because checksum validation detects unhealthy copies rather than selecting request hosts. Move 5.2 "Three-copy push quorum" to Update Coordination Protocol, and move 5.4 "Closest synchronized replica serving" to Repository Request Routing; both are coordination or routing decisions rather than replication topology. These reorganizations would make the server-scale authority, placement, routing, coordination, replication, and maintenance decisions correspond more closely to their values.

Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy correctly uses JSON dimensions, distinguishes accepted/rejected candidates from outcomes, and every dimension has at least two candidate values, with several choices grounded in scale, consistency, latency, availability, and storage constraints. However, many dimensions combine multiple decision questions. In dimension 1, 'Repository Authority Model' mixes authority storage choices (1.1–1.3) with a consistency property (1.4); move 1.4 to the coordination/consistency decision. Dimension 21, "Repository Mutation Protocol," combines replica commit, write ordering, and the S3 synchronization primitive; split it into distinct commit and ordering/coordination decisions. These reorganizations are important for the requested server- and client-side architecture taxonomy for very many, very large repositories and users.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Several dimensions contain multiple decision questions despite the otherwise relevant server/client scaling scope. (1) Dimension 13, Client Performance Configuration, mixes configuration policy (13.1-13.2), implementation/distribution (13.3-13.4), and separate maintenance settings (13.5-13.7); split the first two into decision points with two values each and remove or move the remaining singleton decisions to matching existing dimensions. (2) Dimension 17, Repository Host Selection, combines location mechanisms (17.1-17.2), replica-routing policies (17.4-17.5), and checksum validation metadata (17.3); split the first two groups and move 17.3 to the existing replica-validation decision. (3) Dimension 28, Read Validation and Catch-up, combines consistency/read validation (28.1, 28.3) with catch-up signaling and execution (28.2, 28.4); split those into two dimensions, retaining at least two candidates in each. (4) Dimension 20, Replica Write Quorum, mixes quorum size (20.1, 20.2, 20.4) with admission behavior when quorum is unavailable (20.3, 20.5); split these questions. (5) Dimension 29, Repository Replica Count and Sizing, includes the throughput target 29.3, which is a constraint/target rather than a replica-count alternative; remove it from the candidate decisions. The other dimensions generally have at least two candidate decisions answering a recognizable mechanism or policy question, and outcome values are appropriately distinguishable from candidates.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and the outcome values in dimensions 29, 28, 31, and 17 are described as effects rather than alternatives. However, several mixed values are described as adopted: 31.2 "Layered distributed repository replication" says the approach was adopted, 28.1 "Fully consistent repository views" says views are maintained, 18.4 "Git-protocol repository access" says repositories use it, and 13.3 "Custom Git distribution" says it supplies capabilities. For each, either change the status to accepted if adoption is intended, or rewrite the description to explicitly preserve the source disagreement. No clear duplicate candidate or outcome-as-alternative violation is otherwise evident.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy places nearly all decision-bearing passages under existing dimensions, including client performance configuration (13), replication and sizing (31, 29), serving and host selection (18, 17), and mutation/quorum protocols (21, 20). The main uncovered decision is s03_p07: planned maintenance uses server quiescing so long-running reads finish while writes continue during reboot. Add a planned-maintenance or graceful-shutdown dimension/value for quiescing and write/read handling, supported by s03_p07 (and the rolling-reboot policy in s03_p08).

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many major adopted Spokes choices, including application-level replication (31.1), three replicas and throughput goals (29.1 and 29.3), rendezvous hashing and nearest synchronized reads (17.2 and 17.5), three-phase commit and quorum-based writes (21.1, 20.2, and 20.4), and Scalar's automatic configuration and background fetches (13.1 and 13.5). Missing options requiring revision are: (1) add "Git partial clone" to dimension 18, Repository Serving Mechanism, supported by s04_p01 and s04_p02; (2) add client-maintenance values such as sparse-checkout cone mode, background incremental maintenance/GC, loose-object cleanup, and multi-pack-index maintenance to dimension 13, Client Performance Configuration, supported by s04_p02, s05_p04, s05_p09, and s05_p12; (3) add rejected "block-level filesystem replication" and the rejected distributed-filesystem/packfile approaches to dimension 31, Repository Replication Mechanism, supported by s02_p02, s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05; (4) add a value for coalescing bookkeeping updates and prioritizing user-initiated updates to dimension 21, Repository Mutation Protocol, supported by s02_p06; and (5) add a maintenance-lifecycle dimension covering quiescing before reboot, rolling reboot, and graceful replica retirement, supported by s03_p07, s03_p08, and s03_p09. Dimension 20 also lacks the non-voting geo-replica option described in s02_p06.

criteria.name: Value exclusivity
criteria.description: Each system (source) adopts one value per dimension: the values of a dimension are alternatives, not features used together. Deterministic: computed from the evidence, without a judge.
criteria.reason:
- Dimension 17 'Repository Host Selection': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 17.3 'Continuous checksum routing metadata' and 17.5 'Closest synchronized replica serving' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p07, s01_p09, s02_p05).
- Dimension 20 'Replica Write Quorum': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 20.1 'Three-copy push quorum' and 20.3 'Durability-prioritized write admission' are adopted together by s02, s03 (passages s02_p01, s03_p01, s03_p02).
- Dimension 21 'Repository Mutation Protocol': 3 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 21.1 'Three-phase commit' and 21.4 'Advanced consensus coordination' are adopted together by s01, s02 (passages s01_p07, s01_p08, s02_p03).
- Dimension 13 'Client Performance Configuration': 2 of 3 sources adopt several of its values. Values 13.1 'Automatic performance configuration' and 13.3 'Custom Git distribution' are adopted together by s04, s05 (passages s04_p01, s04_p02, s05_p01).
Values one source uses together are not alternatives. Split such a dimension into the questions its values answer (every part keeps at least two candidate decisions), move a value to the existing dimension whose question it answers, or merge two values that are the same option.
